Patient demographics:
  age: 19
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Fast Food Worker
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 40

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction, Avoid Stressors: avoid anything that could be stressful, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
  Negative Appraisals: Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me, Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse

Vignette:
Ethan, a 19-year-old, remembered the day the tornado tore through his town with a chilling clarity that always brought the same terror he’d felt then. He had been working the late shift at Burger Blast, wiping down counters, when the sky outside had turned an unnatural, sickly green. The storm sirens had blared, a sound that now made his stomach clench, but before he could even process it, the world had exploded. He remembered the deafening roar, like a freight train barreling through the restaurant, the building shaking violently, the shattering glass of the drive-thru window, and the sudden, gut-wrenching lurch as the roof peeled away. He’d thrown himself under a metal counter, covering his head, the air thick with the smell of wet earth, fried grease, and a sharp, acrid scent he couldn't quite place, but which now sometimes accompanied the visual memories that flooded his mind. He saw images of splintered wood, twisted metal, and the chaotic swirl of debris against that ominous green sky, and each time, the feeling of absolute helplessness and impending doom washed over him anew.

In the weeks and months that followed, Ethan found himself constantly battling against these intrusive images and sensations. He tried hard not to think about the tornado, pushing the memories away whenever they surfaced, but they were persistent. The smell of rain on hot asphalt, the sudden gust of wind, or even the familiar scent of the deep fryer at work could trigger a vivid flashback, complete with the terrifying smells and sights of that day. He started avoiding anything that might bring on these feelings. He stopped watching the local news, especially weather reports, and would take circuitous routes to work to avoid streets where the damage had been most severe, even though they’d long since been cleared.

His job at Burger Blast, once a simple way to earn money, became a minefield of potential stressors. The clatter of a dropped tray would make him jump, and the whir of the industrial milkshake machine could sometimes mimic the rising roar of the wind. Most challenging, though, were the customer interactions. He’d always been a bit quiet, but now, the thought of an unscripted conversation filled him with dread. Before every shift, before approaching the counter, and even before answering a simple question from a coworker, he found himself rehearsing what to say, running through scenarios in his head, trying to anticipate every possible response. This made him slow, often hesitant, and he noticed his manager started giving him fewer shifts at the front counter, assigning him to stock shelves or clean the back kitchen instead. He felt increasingly isolated, watching his coworkers chat easily while he struggled to formulate even simple sentences.

What frightened Ethan most was the creeping realization that he felt fundamentally different. He used to be a happy person, enjoying video games and hanging out with his friends, but now he was always miserable, a heavy cloud of sadness settling over him that he couldn't shake. He looked in the mirror and felt a profound sense of alienation, believing that the person he had become was utterly unrecognisable to him. He was certain that the tornado had permanently changed him for the worse, leaving an indelible mark that could never be erased. This belief fueled his avoidance, making him think there was no point in trying to engage with life as he once had. He knew he was struggling, knew he wasn't himself, and the constant effort to suppress his thoughts and avoid triggers was exhausting. It was this pervasive sense of being lost, of his old self being irretrievably gone, that finally led him to search for help, hoping against his own conviction that perhaps, somehow, a part of him could still be found.
